::: {.lead}
In *Torch Hall*, a dungeon game, the designer writes the rules in plain
words: "The chest opens if the player has the key and no skeleton is near,
or the player is a thief." "A weak guard flees; otherwise it attacks a
player it sees near, or chases a player it sees." Words are easy to read
but not exact: does "or" include both? Which rule wins when two are true?
In lectures 16–18 you learned propositions, truth tables and Boolean
algebra. In this lesson you **apply** them: you turn words into exact
conditions, read if-then rules correctly, list every case in a decision
table, put else-if rules in the right order, model a guard as a state
machine, and test the rules at their borders. Every section ends with a
short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary implication sufficient-condition necessary-condition contrapositive decision-table else-if-chain unreachable-rule state-machine edge-case test-case >}}

## 19.1 From words to conditions

A designer's rule becomes code only when every word has one exact meaning
(@fig-words).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.1 — Translating rule words"}
- **and** → ∧ (`&&`); **or** → ∨ (`||`), which includes "both";
  **not, no, without** → ¬ (`!`).
- **either … or, but not both** → ⊕ (`^`).
- **unless p** → "if not p".
- **only if q** → q is needed: … → q.

First give each fact a letter, then find the main operator: the word that
joins the two big parts of the sentence.
:::

![Rule words and their logic.](images/rule-words.png){#fig-words width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.1 — The chest of Torch Hall"}
"The chest opens if the player has the key and no skeleton is near, or the
player is a thief."

1. Letters: k = has the key, s = a skeleton is near, t = is a thief.
2. The comma before "or" splits the sentence: (key and no skeleton) **or**
   thief.
3. Condition: (k ∧ ¬s) ∨ t, in code `(hasKey && !skeletonNear) || isThief`.
4. Check one case: a thief without a key, with a skeleton near: k = F, s =
   T, t = T gives F ∨ T = **T**. The chest opens, as the designer wants.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.2 — Unless"}
"The bridge stays up unless the lever is pulled." With l = the lever is
pulled: bridgeUp = ¬l. In code `bool bridgeUp = !leverPulled;`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Ignoring the brackets that the sentence implies. k ∧ (¬s ∨ t) looks
similar, but a thief without a key can never open the chest with it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Translate"}
Write as a condition, with your own letters: (a) "The trap fires when the
player steps on the plate and is not flying." (b) "The door opens with the
red key or the blue key, but not both." (c) "The alarm rings unless the
guard is asleep."

*Your result:* three conditions.
:::

## 19.2 If-then rules: sufficient and necessary

Many rules have the form "if p, then q". The implication of lecture 16
tells us exactly what such a rule promises (@fig-imp).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.2 — Sufficient, necessary, contrapositive"}
In the rule p → q:

- p is a **sufficient condition** for q: when p is true, q is surely true.
- q is a **necessary condition** for p: without q, p cannot be true.
- The **contrapositive** ¬q → ¬p is equivalent to p → q.
- The **converse** q → p is **not** equivalent to p → q.

"p only if q" means p → q. "p if and only if q" means p → q and q → p.
:::

![The implication, its contrapositive and its converse.](images/implication.png){#fig-imp width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.3 — The crown and the gate"}
Rule: "If the player holds the crown, the gate is open" (crown → open).

1. The gate is shut. By the contrapositive, the player does **not** hold
   the crown.
2. The gate is open. We know **nothing** about the crown: someone may have
   opened it with a lever. The converse is not the rule.
3. Only the case crown = T, open = F breaks the rule. A tester looks for
   exactly this case.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.4 — Only if"}
"The player may enter the boss room only if all three torches are lit":
enter → lit. A player in the boss room means the torches are lit. But lit
torches alone do not let the player in; maybe a key is also needed.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading p → q as q → p. "If you hold the crown, the gate is open" does not
mean "if the gate is open, you hold the crown".
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · What follows?"}
Rule: "If the boss is defeated, the music changes." Say what follows in
each case: (a) the boss is defeated; (b) the music did not change; (c) the
music changed.

*Your result:* three short answers.
:::

## 19.3 Decision tables

When a decision depends on several conditions, a **decision table** lists
every case and the action for it (@fig-dt).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.3 — Decision table"}
A **decision table** has one column for each condition, one row for each
combination of truth values (2^n rows for n conditions), and the action of
the game in that row. A good table is **complete** (every row has an
action) and has **no conflicts** (no row has two actions).
:::

![The decision table of the guard.](images/decision-table.png){#fig-dt width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.5 — The guard of Torch Hall"}
Conditions: s = the guard sees the player, n = the player is near, w = the
guard is weak (health < 30). The designer's words: "A weak guard flees;
otherwise it attacks a player it sees near, or chases a player it sees;
otherwise it patrols."

1. 3 conditions → 8 rows.
2. Every row with w = T: **Flee** (4 rows).
3. w = F, s = T, n = T: **Attack**. w = F, s = T, n = F: **Chase**.
4. w = F, s = F: **Patrol** (2 rows). All 8 rows have exactly one action.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing only the cases you think of. The designer forgot "weak and sees the
player": the table shows the missing row at once.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A trap table"}
A spike trap fires when the plate is pressed (p) and the trap is armed (a),
unless the player is flying (f). Make the decision table with 8 rows and
the action "fire" or "wait".

*Your result:* a table; in how many rows does it fire?
:::

## 19.4 Else-if chains: the order matters

In code, a decision table often becomes an **else-if chain**. The chain is
read from the top, and the **first** true rule wins (@fig-order).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.4 — Else-if chain and unreachable rule"}
In an **else-if chain**, only the first rule whose condition is true runs;
the `else` at the end catches every other case. A rule is **unreachable**
when the rules above it catch all of its cases; it never runs. Put the
**most important** and the **most specific** rules first.
:::

![The same rules in a wrong and a right order.](images/rule-order.png){#fig-order width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.6 — The guard in code"}
A programmer writes `if (s) Chase(); else if (s && n) Attack(); else if (w)
Flee(); else Patrol();`

1. Every case with s is caught by Chase: **Attack never runs**.
2. Row s = T, w = T: the chain says Chase, the table says Flee.
3. Fix: `if (w) Flee(); else if (s && n) Attack(); else if (s) Chase();
   else Patrol();` Now the chain gives the table in all 8 rows.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/guard-brain.html" poster="sims/guard-brain.png" title="Guard Brain: rules, order and the decision table" height="900" >}}

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
void Decide() {
    if (health < 30)                Flee();
    else if (seesPlayer && isNear)  Attack();
    else if (seesPlayer)            Chase();
    else                            Patrol();
}
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Putting the general rule (`if (seesPlayer)`) before the special one
(`seesPlayer && isNear`). The special rule becomes unreachable.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Order the rules"}
1. In **Guard Brain**, switch on s and n. Which action runs?
2. Change the order until the chain and the designer agree in all 8 rows.

*Your result:* the right order of the three rules.
:::

## 19.5 The guard as a state machine

A real guard does not forget what it did a moment ago. Many games model
such characters as **state machines** (@fig-fsm).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.5 — State machine"}
A **state machine** has a few **states** (Patrol, Chase, Attack, Flee) and
**transitions**: arrows from one state to another, each with a condition.
In every frame, the character checks only the conditions on the arrows
that leave its current state.
:::

![The guard as a state machine.](images/guard-states.png){#fig-fsm width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.7 — One step of the guard"}
The guard is in **Chase**. The arrows that leave Chase are n (→ Attack),
¬s (→ Patrol) and w (→ Flee).

1. The player comes near: n = T → **Attack**.
2. The player runs away: in Attack, ¬n = T → back to **Chase**.
3. The guard is hit and its health falls to 25: w = T → **Flee**.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
switch (state) {
    case State.Patrol: if (weak) state = State.Flee;  else if (sees) state = State.Chase;  break;
    case State.Chase:  if (weak) state = State.Flee;  else if (near) state = State.Attack; else if (!sees) state = State.Patrol; break;
    case State.Attack: if (weak) state = State.Flee;  else if (!near) state = State.Chase;  break;
}
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Two arrows from one state that can be true together, with no order: the
guard in Chase with w and n both true. Check the order of the conditions on
each state, like in an else-if chain.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Follow the guard"}
Start in Patrol. Follow the guard through these frames and write its state
each time: (1) s; (2) s, n; (3) s, ¬n; (4) ¬s; (5) w.

*Your result:* five states.
:::

## 19.6 Testing rules with edge cases

A rule is only right when the code gives the right action in **every**
case. Truth tables give the test cases; numbers need **edge cases** too
(@fig-edge).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 19.6 — Test cases and edge cases"}
A **test case** is one input with the expected result: for logic rules,
one row of the decision table. An **edge case** is a test at the border of
a number rule: for "health < 30", test 29, **30** and 31.
:::

![Testing at the border of the rule.](images/edge-cases.png){#fig-edge width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.8 — The bug at 30"}
The rule says the guard flees when health < 30. The code says
`if (health <= 30) Flee();`.

1. health = 10 and health = 80: the code and the rule agree. These tests
   find nothing.
2. health = **30**: the rule says fight, the code says flee. The bug is
   found.
3. Fix: `health < 30`, and keep the test with 30 for the next version.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Testing only "normal" values in the middle. Bugs hide at the borders: `<`
or `<=`, `>` or `>=`.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Edge cases"}
The rule: "A coin gives a bonus life when the player has at least 100
coins and less than 3 lives." Write four edge-case tests (coins and lives)
with the expected result.

*Your result:* four test cases.
:::

## Case study: Rule Smith

The designer of *Torch Hall* gives six rules in words and code: the chest
rule with the thief; the bridge that stays up unless the lever is pulled;
the boss room that a player may enter only if the torches are lit; the
crown and the gate; a guard chain with an unreachable rule; and the flee
rule with `<=`. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
rules. In the mini-game below you turn each one into an exact condition or
find its bug.

{{< sim file="sims/rule-smith.html" poster="sims/rule-smith.png" title="Rule Smith: exact rules, no bugs" kind="game" height="560" >}}

## Further reading

Rosen, *Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications*, 8th ed., Section 1.1
(conditional statements, converse and contrapositive) and Section 1.2
(applications). Millington, *AI for Games*, 3rd ed., Chapter 5 (decision
making, decision trees and state machines).

## Exercises

1. Translate: "The lift moves when the button is pressed and the door is
   closed."
2. Translate: "The shop is open unless it is night."
3. Translate: "The player wins with the gold or the gem, but not both."
4. In the rule p → q, which condition is sufficient and which is necessary?
5. Write the contrapositive of "If the player is invisible, the guard does
   not see the player."
6. Rule: crown → gate open. The gate is open. Does the player hold the
   crown?
7. "You may cast the spell only if you have 10 mana." Write it as an
   implication.
8. How many rows has a decision table with 4 conditions?
9. What makes a decision table complete? What is a conflict?
10. In an else-if chain, which rule runs when two conditions are true?
11. Why is `else if (s && n)` unreachable after `if (s)`?
12. Order these rules: `Patrol()` (else), `Flee()` if w, `Chase()` if s.
13. In the state machine of @fig-fsm, the guard is in Attack and the
    player walks away. What is the next state?
14. Which three health values do you test for the rule "health < 30"?
15. The rule is "speed > 5". The code says `speed >= 5`. Which test finds
    the bug?
16. Write the decision table of the chest rule (k ∧ ¬s) ∨ t. In how many
    rows does it open?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. b ∧ c (button pressed and door closed).
2. open = ¬night.
3. g ⊕ m.
4. p is sufficient for q; q is necessary for p.
5. If the guard sees the player, the player is not invisible.
6. We cannot know: the converse is not the rule.
7. cast → mana ≥ 10.
8. 2⁴ = 16.
9. Complete: every row has an action. Conflict: a row with two actions.
10. The first true rule from the top.
11. Every case with s and n also has s, so `if (s)` catches it first.
12. `if (w) Flee(); else if (s) Chase(); else Patrol();`
13. Chase (¬n).
14. 29, 30 and 31.
15. speed = 5.
16. It opens in 5 of 8 rows: the 4 rows with t, and k = T, s = F, t = F.
:::
